Hi!

I recently ported the ZeroFS (https://github.com/Barre/ZeroFS) userspace filesystem client to an out-of-tree Linux kernel module written in
Rust (https://github.com/Barre/ZeroFS/tree/main/kernel).

It uses netfslib (https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/netfs_library.html) and currently supports:

  • Mounting, lookup, attributes, directory iteration, and statfs
  • File and directory creation, rename, unlink, hard and symbolic links, device nodes, and FIFOs
  • Persistent opens and atomic_open
  • Buffered I/O, dirty-folio writeback, writable mmap, and direct I/O
  • fallocate, SEEK_DATA, SEEK_HOLE, POSIX record locks, flock, and fsync

The build also has a self-contained path for a limited set of supported kernels built with CONFIG_RUST=n.

I thought this might be of particular interest to people here, and I’d be interested in feedback on the overall approach.

Thanks!

Interesting!

It would be nice to see VFS work restart in upstream, not sure if you are considering that.

One thing I noticed from the blog post:

Most distribution kernels are built without Rust support

Some major distributions like Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian (testing), Arch and Nix enable CONFIG_RUST. Android too. Of course, it is not universal, but those are already a big set. (Well, as far as I recall, I may be out-of-date)

Some major distributions like Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian (testing), Arch and Nix enable CONFIG_RUST. Android too. Of course, it is not universal, but those are already a big set. (Well, as far as I recall, I may be out-of-date)

Indeed, but I wanted to ship to as many as "current" mainstream distros as possible.

It would be nice to see VFS work restart in upstream, not sure if you are considering that.

Ultimately, I'd _love_ to be able to upstream this work. I'm not sure how that'd work though, I guess I'd have to upstream bindings for VFS and netfslib, then probably https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/adding-new-filesystems.html?

I also saw https://github.com/Rust-for-Linux/linux/pull/1222 but I am not sure what's the current state?

Indeed, but I wanted to ship to as many as "current" mainstream distros as possible.

Yeah, of course, that is understandable -- I was only referring to the phrase itself, i.e. nowadays I probably wouldn't say "most distributions" disable it (but I guess it depends on how one counts).

Ultimately, I'd _love_ to be able to upstream this work. I'm not sure how that'd work though, I guess I'd have to upstream bindings for VFS and netfslib

Yeah, first the abstractions go in, and that usually takes time on its own. Normally there needs to be a user for that to happen, i.e. to showcase how the abstractions work, even if they are samples (e.g. an example filesystem or ideally a simple existing one re-implemented in Rust for comparison with C, even if those don't land; see as well https://rust-for-linux.com/rust-reference-drivers).

Now, landing a new filesystem is another discussion of its own, but since there has been interest in Rust filesystems for a while, it may be doable to land the abstractions independently of the decision on the new filesystem.

I also saw https://github.com/Rust-for-Linux/linux/pull/1222 but I am not sure what's the current state?

Hard to say -- I would suggest pinging the author. There have been several efforts around VFS in the past, though, and there are also others out-of-tree that may be interested in helping given their interest in Rust.
About things like netfslib, would they warrant a pure rust reimplementation or just bindings?

Normally, I would expect abstractions rather than re-implementations. Sometimes there may be reasons to do re-implementations, but it is rare (do you think there is a good reason to go that way in this case?).

In any case, it depends on the netfs maintainers.
